posts.title: 🚀 iGEM Essay Contest
posts.author: @tarmaska_11
posts.abstract: Every iGEM project has a story behind it. Send us yours by 14 November - the best submissions will be published here on 15 November.
posts.body:
Your iGEM story deserves to be heard!

Every iGEM project has a story behind it - scientific breakthroughs, unexpected challenges, failed experiments, memorable moments, and lessons worth sharing. Now, we want to give those stories a place to be heard.

We're inviting iGEMers from across the community to share their experiences, projects, and personal journeys.

How to participate?

  1. Write a post about your iGEM journey, project, experience, or anything you think the community would find interesting.
  2. Send your submission to tarmaska11@gmail.com.
  3. Submit it by 14 November, 23:59 (France time).

P.S. - Yes, you may attach photos & illustrations.

What happens next?

We'll select the best submissions and publish them directly on the {{name}} website on 15 November, making your stories accessible to the wider iGEM community.

Whether it's a scientific achievement, a funny behind-the-scenes story, a lesson learned, or a personal reflection - we want to hear it!

Your experience could inspire the next generation of iGEMers. Share your story and become part of the community's collective knowledge.

We look forward to reading your submissions!

posts.title: Welcome to the iGEM Intelligence Machine
posts.author: @tarmaska_11
posts.abstract: A quick guide to the archive: how search, summaries, embedded wikis and the Ask AI chat work - what to keep in mind while using them, and where the archive is heading next.
posts.body:
Every year hundreds of iGEM teams reinvent the same wheels. Someone has probably already tried your chassis, your promoter, or your exact failure mode, but that knowledge is spread over thousands of wikis that no search engine will find for you.

Lucky you, you stumbled upon this site.

This is a single searchable archive of every iGEM project from {{first_year}} to {{last_year}} - {{projects}} projects in total. Search by idea, chassis organism, molecular technique, biological part, keywords or concepts - it has it all.

Search

Here's a quick tutorial on how to use it. Take the keyword "Spider" as an example - what happens when you hit search?

You get a list of 236 teams: 34 of them are actually about spiders. The first teams in the list matched in their summary, while the remaining 202 matched only in their raw wiki text.

The difference is subtle, but important: a match in the summary almost guarantees that spiders were one of the main aspects of the project, while a raw wiki match only means that spiders were mentioned somewhere in the team's wiki - not necessarily as a major part of the project.

Summary matches are marked with a star ★ and shown at the top of the list. Raw wiki matches follow after them, each labelled "Matched: X times" and sorted in descending order, so you can estimate their relevance at a glance.

The search bar has two modes:

  • Keyword (default) - exact keyword matching. It finds every project that contains your words, ranked by how well they match.
  • Concept + Keyword - shows all the same keyword matches first, and then adds projects that are about the same thing, even if they never use your exact words. These extra results are marked "related" (for "spider", it brings the list up to 263 teams). Use it when you're exploring an idea rather than looking for one specific term.

Combining words: AND and OR

When you type several words, a team has to mention all of them: spider silk finds 118 teams instead of 236 for "spider" alone. Writing spider AND silk means exactly the same thing - use whichever reads better to you.

To widen the search instead, put OR between the alternatives: spider OR coffee finds 786 teams that mention either one. Each side of an OR is its own little search, so arsenic biosensor OR mercury biosensor finds biosensors for either metal.

You don't need to worry about capital letters, plurals or common spelling variants: "mussel" also finds "mussels", and "E. coli" also finds "Escherichia coli".

One more handy detail: every search has its own web address - your words, filters and mode included - so you can bookmark it or send it straight to a teammate.

Filters

Next to the results you'll find filters: Team section, Year, Village and Chassis, with Target molecule, Molecular technique, Biological part, Region and Country hidden under "More filters". You can tick several values at once and combine them with any search - for example, every 2023-2025 project that used yeast.

Summary

Click any team and its summary will open up. It contains:

  • Problem - the real-world problem the team set out to solve;
  • Approach - how they decided to tackle it;
  • Summary - a short abstract of their work;
  • Target molecules - the molecules the project produces, detects or degrades, useful for finding everyone who has worked on "your" molecule;
  • Chassis organisms - the organisms they engineered (E. coli, yeast, B. subtilis, cell-free systems, etc.);
  • Molecular techniques - the lab and design methods they used (cloning methods, CRISPR, directed evolution, modelling, etc.);
  • Biological parts - the parts they built or used, linked to the iGEM Registry wherever a BBa code exists;
  • Key results - what actually worked and what they managed to show;
  • Failure modes - what went wrong, didn't work or couldn't be finished. Often the most valuable section, since it can save you months of repeating the same mistakes;
  • Novelty claim - the most important one in my opinion: what the team says is new about their project compared to everything done before;
  • Key references - the main papers and sources they built their work on.

This summary is constructed in such a way that you, as a quick viewer, can grasp the basic idea of a team's research at a glance and figure out whether it fits your research or not.

Keep in mind: these summaries were not written by hand. They were generated by AI, so they may not be precise, and the inner workings of every project are undoubtedly far more complex.

Instead, I suggest you use them as a quick reference to understand what a project is about without even opening the wiki - and if it looks relevant, go to the wiki itself for the details.

For generation, we used the following AI models:

  • Gemini - 323 projects (6.5%);
  • GitHub Copilot - 239 projects (4.8%);
  • Codex - 202 projects (4.1%);
  • Claude - 6 projects (0.1%);
  • Gemma 3n E4B (local) - 4,208 projects (84.5%).

We tried to strive for quality, so we initially used free cloud AI services. However, it proved unsustainable to summarize all ~5,000 projects that way in time, so we switched to a local solution: we ran the Gemma 3n E4B model on our own computer 24/7 for two weeks, with a 32k context window to fit the entirety of most wikis. This allowed us to get a summary for every single project, but the quality of these summaries is more surface-level: they can miss details, mix up minor facts or describe the project more generally than the larger cloud models do. With the rapid advancement of LLM technologies, we believe that in the coming years we'll be able to provide much more detailed and accurate project descriptions for future teams.

Still, it's enough to grasp the main idea. At the very top of every summary you'll see additional details: the project's field and track (village); Country/City; Team section; "src" - the AI model that generated the summary; and a link to the original wiki on the web.

Wiki view

Now, the interesting part: since the iGEM Intelligence Machine is meant to be the ultimate tool for fast screening of projects relevant to your research, we decided to embed the iGEM wikis directly.

Essentially, it allows you to view a team's wiki right on our website, without opening another browser tab, and you can fully interact with it - scroll, click, navigate between pages.

How it works: open any team and switch to the "Wiki + Ask AI" tab. The wiki opens on the left, the AI chat on the right. Above the wiki you can switch between two views:

  • Live wiki / Archived wiki - the actual web page of the wiki;
  • Saved text - the full text of the wiki that we collected and stored ourselves. It always works, even when the web page doesn't, and it has its own search box (Ctrl+F) to jump straight to the part you need.

All teams are divided into "before 2022" and "from 2022 on", because in 2022 iGEM moved all wikis to a new system.

Teams before 2022 - their wikis still live on the old igem.org pages, but igem.org doesn't allow its pages to be embedded on other websites. So instead, we show you the copy saved by the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine, which preserves the history of the internet. It can take a few seconds to load. The saved text for these years was also collected from the old igem.org pages and the Wayback Machine. Some wikis from earlier years were never fully archived, so a few teams might be lost, and some saved pages may be incomplete or miss parts of the project.

Teams from 2022 on were collected directly from iGEM's GitLab, by downloading all the wiki repositories and extracting the pure text from their code. This allowed us to fully cover the content of every wiki, so they are much more complete and reliable. Their live wikis are embedded directly from the official wiki system and will stay stable as long as the current iGEM system does.

Keep in mind: most wikis were never designed to be embedded, so some of them may look weird or break inside our page. In that case, click "Open in new tab ↗" above the wiki (or the "open wiki ↗" link in the summary) to open the original wiki in a new tab.

AI feature

Next to every wiki there is an "Ask AI" chat. It answers questions about that one specific project, using only that team's summary and saved wiki text - so you can ask things like "What chassis did they use?", "Which experiments failed and why?" or "How did they measure their results?" and get an answer without reading the whole wiki. It remembers the conversation, so you can ask follow-up questions too.

The chat works with your own API key. By default it uses Google's Gemini models, which you can use for free:

  1. Go to aistudio.google.com/apikey and sign in with your Google account.
  2. Click "Create API key" - no billing or card needed.
  3. Paste the key into the box in the Ask AI panel.

Your key is saved only in your own browser and is never sent to us - your questions go straight from your browser to Google. The free tier has per-minute and per-day limits, so if it stops answering, wait a bit and try again.

Gemini is not the only option. In the Provider list you can switch to Groq (also free), OpenRouter, OpenAI or Anthropic Claude, and "Other" accepts any OpenAI-compatible service - so the chat never depends on a single company. Whichever you pick gets exactly the same project summary and wiki text to answer from, and each service keeps its own key. Click ⓘ next to the key box for a quick guide to getting one.

Same as with the summaries: AI can make mistakes. If an answer matters for your project, double-check it in the wiki - the saved text search makes that quick.

Future aspirations

Today the iGEM Intelligence Machine holds every project from {{first_year}} to {{last_year}} - the whole history of the competition as it stands right now. But iGEM never stands still. Every season brings hundreds of new teams, new wikis and new ideas, and this archive is built to grow with them.

The data lives in its own open database, separate from the website, so it can keep moving even after the site itself is frozen. In the coming years we plan to add each new season's teams, fill in the wikis that were only partly archived, and re-summarize older projects with better AI models as they appear - turning today's surface-level summaries into the detailed descriptions every project deserves.

And we don't want to be the only ones building on it. We know ours won't stay the best way to search iGEM's history for long - people will find smarter ways to search, compare and analyse these projects than we can imagine today. That's why everything this website runs on is yours: press Database at the top of the page to download the whole archive, load it into your own scripts, feed it to an AI, and look for patterns we never thought to look for. If you build something with it, share it back with the community - that's how iGEM works.

Every team in this archive started exactly where you are now: with a question and a blank page. Thousands of them have already left their answers, their results and their mistakes behind, so you never have to start from zero.

We stand on the shoulders of giants, don't we?

Let's build something scientifish!✨️
